title: The Trinity's undivided work and the righteous one's hope
english: Then God is spoken of in divine terms as the Creator, and the creation is the work of the Word and the Spirit. It is clear that the words are human, since a mouth is mentioned from which word and spirit come, but they are understood differently when applied to God, according to his uncompounded and entirely bodiless nature. That is, the Word exists with God who exists, and the Spirit exists. The Word is the manifestation of the Father, and for this reason he is named Word. The Spirit is the participation in the Word, as Spirit from the mouth. When he says heavens and powers of the heavens, he does not divide the creation, assigning the heavens to the Word and the powers to the Spirit, for the works of the Trinity are undivided. Rather, he expresses the same thing in different ways. As in the verse, Jacob entered into Egypt and Israel sojourned in the land of Ham, the entrance does not refer to one person, Jacob, and the dwelling to another, Israel. The parallel expresses the same thing, and we would find this custom in many places.

On Psalm 33:7 (34:7). David, showing himself, says that he became poor, that he was in anguish in his flight, and that he escaped this danger by the will of God, since the scheme of madness would not otherwise have prevailed if not for God's will.

On Psalm 33:9 (34:9). He uses taste metaphorically for the experience of things, which was present to him at that time. What happened to him through God's goodness, that he was not overlooked while being pursued by a foreign king but was saved from two most severe and powerful enemies, this he sets before all in common, as something that did not happen only to him but would also happen to others, as many as join themselves to God through hope in God. Blessedness must consist in this, and in nothing else, as David says in the verse, Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful.

On Psalm 33:20 (34:20). He commands us to look to the end and to take courage in the release from afflictions, not to be distressed at the beginning itself whenever affliction happens to occur. For the soul must be prepared in this way, not as one that will not suffer, but as one that will not be defeated by its sufferings.

On Psalm 34:1-3 (35:1-3). He shapes the speech about God into complete likeness of a human being, as Isaiah also does, in order to show that what is impossible in him is possible for God, asking him to wage war and to be armed with shield and spear and to shut off the attacks of enemies with a middle wall. Isaiah also shows this in Christ, foreseeing him coming from the punishment of the unjust with his garment reddened from the slaughter of the foreigners: Who is this who has come from Edom, redness of garments from Bozrah, and the rest? (Isaiah 63:1). So the things that are referred to the Father in divine terms clearly belong to the Son and are fulfilled in the Son.

On Psalm 34:5 (35:5). That they become invisible is turned against them, like dust driven by the wind. They are driven out not by a human hand, for the righteous suffer this rather at the hands of the unjust, but this happens through angels, as the Lord says: The holy ones will go out and will choose the unjust from the midst of the righteous and will separate them (Matthew 13:49). For now the discordant elements are mixed together, but then they will be divided according to the difference of their manner, according to what was said again by the Savior: And many dwelling places are with my Father (John 14:2).

On Psalm 34:6 (35:6). The ways of the impious, he says, are dark; they do not know how they advance. He asks that this be accomplished, praying that the deed of the unjust be held in darkness, since it belongs to darkness, and that they fall after slipping, because they walk a slippery road, for nothing in injustice has firmness, and that they become invisible, pursued by angels, which is what they themselves do against the righteous.

On Psalm 34:13 (35:13). He flees, he says, to his own strength, which is God. For a person seeks God with fastings and humiliations, turning the whole soul to invocations of God through freedom from bodily pleasures, when the invocations linger in the mind during prayer and slip into the bosom of the soul.

On Psalm 35:6 (36:6). For the things ordered by God are firm and unshaken, such as what was said to Noah, that he would no longer bring a flood for the destruction of living creatures, which agrees with the word about God's forbearance. For the firmness of the word has been fixed forever, being great and manifest. So also whatever else has been ordered and fixed according to the righteousness and goodness of God has a solid and unshaken permanence forever. Such is also the verse, Once I swore in my holy one, if I will lie to David (Psalm 88:36 (89:35)). To this also tends the saying, For the gifts of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29).
On Psalm 35:7a (36:7a). Again he compares the height of righteousness to mountains.

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 33 (34), explaining that the psalm's human-sounding words about God's mouth and word must be understood spiritually, and then moving through the psalm's verses on the righteous person's deliverance.

title: God's retribution is certain and the righteous must wait in hope
english: This carries a threat of retributions, because it is impossible for anything to happen contrary to what is just when righteousness is the overseer of what takes place. So even those who now escape the punishing retributions, or who do not receive their retributions, will certainly receive them later. And this is unchangeable with God, as Paul said with confidence that God, the righteous judge, will give him the crown of righteousness on that day (2 Timothy 4:8).
On Psalm 35:10a (36:9a). The things that lead to life are supplied abundantly by God, and if they were not supplied, life would be destroyed.

On Psalm 35:10b (36:9b). He is illuminated, he says, by the light from heaven, by the one who set the sun as the light of day. But these things are common to the righteous and the unrighteous, and in them he marveled at God's philanthropy, since the ungrateful are not excluded from enjoying what comes from God. But what is exceptional and proper to God's own is something else.

On Psalm 36:7 (37:7). He commands to be still and wait for God, not being disturbed by present things but hoping for future things, according to the apostolic word: Rejoicing in hope, enduring in affliction (Romans 12:12), and Jeremiah's word: It is good for a man when he bears a yoke in his youth. He will sit alone and be silent; he will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches.

On Psalm 36:9 (37:9). He commands us to look far off and not be astounded by present things, and to foresee the destruction of the wicked and the preservation of the good. These things clearly reach their end in another age, since the present age does not have the outcomes of these things, but rather the wicked prevail over the things on earth. Therefore he says, The whole world lies in the evil one (1 John 5:19).

On Psalm 36:14ab (37:14ab). He says that the wicked set in motion against themselves the very things they prepare against the righteous, as if someone drew a sword and was slain by it, and the plot too will be futile, like a bow shattered in the hand of an archer. In David's case this was also fulfilled bodily: David struck with their own sword, the one they had drawn against David (cf. 1 Samuel 17:51).

On Psalm 36:27 (37:27). Such an exhortation again comes from the prediction: to flee from evil and practice the doing of good in hope of eternal rest, and the reasoning about the matter is that the overseer is righteous and does not overlook his own.

On Psalm 37:4a (38:4a). He compares his great suffering and many afflictions to a body entirely afflicted, as in Isaiah: From the soles of the feet to the head there is no soundness in it, but wounds and bruises, the burning inflammation of a threat (Isaiah 1:6). These are signs of wrath, and the cause of the wrath is sins, so that the sufferings bring awareness of sins, and in this way they benefit souls, just as bodies are brought from insensibility to sensation.

On Psalm 37:12 (38:12). He laments the desertion of friends and the uprising of enemies, which are also seen in the Savior's sufferings, when the disciples were scattered in fear, and the wicked used every bitterness and malice against him, toward whom he also fulfilled the silence predicted here.

On Psalm 37:14 (38:14). Having, he says, just grounds to answer those who slandered him, but knowing that speech would not be for their benefit, I bore the false accusations without resentment. And as one who does not hear, I was silent, and as one who has no reproof. For what would I say and answer? It was for nothing, as the Lord also said: If I tell you, you will not believe; and if I ask you, you will not answer (Luke 22:67-68). When people do not listen, speech is useless toward them, but useful toward God who hears.

On Psalm 37:22-23 (38:22-23). Human beings would not say these things about themselves, but Christ, in place of human beings and for human beings, suffering as a righteous one at the hands of the unrighteous and taking what is theirs upon himself, would say them: in one place, Why have you forsaken me? in another, Do not forsake me, and Do not depart from me, since this is impossible for him. For I am not alone, he says, because my Father is with me. He asks for the salvation of human beings as his own, having something proper to the request as far as the human element in the mixture with divinity is concerned—this was the passible element naturally united to the flesh—and also having the dignity of the nature that transcends, by which he fulfilled the things of the request.

On Psalm 38:4 (39:4). And hearing, he says, and reckoning up the bold and abusive words of the enemy, and seeing how great an authority of speech he used, to whom it was not fitting even to speak, I was kindled with indignation on behalf of the righteousness that was being dishonored.

On Psalm 38:8a (39:8a). I do not, he says, have anything in myself worthy of expectation, but I wait, expecting what is with you and what is yours, enduring in present labors in hope of future good things.

On Psalm 38:9b (39:9b). I bear, he says, being reproached now and not answering back, knowing in some such way that God wills me to be trained by reproaches. So David himself bore being reviled by Shimei, saying that the Lord had told him to curse David (2 Samuel 16:10).

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 35-38, explaining that God's justice will repay both the wicked and the righteous, and that the righteous must endure present afflictions in hope of future goods.

title: Christ's endurance, resurrection, and the church's hope
english: He speaks of the eternal waiting of the righteous as his own, and of the prayers through which they will hear God accomplish the ascent from Hades, the life made secure forever, and the firm standing in that life amid gladness, brightness, and hymns to God. Such was also the cry in Psalm 29 (30): “I cried to you, and you healed me; you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from those going down to the pit” (Psalm 29:3-4 [30:3-4]), and what follows. In these words he clearly referred Adam’s condition to himself. Then, after bringing in the resurrection, he says at the end: “So that my glory may sing praise to you, and I may not be pierced with sorrow.”

For the things of Christ extend to the salvation of all; they neither happened for his own sake nor stand in him alone. Therefore Paul says: “If the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised” (1 Corinthians 15:16). For if the end for whose sake the cause would have existed had not come about, Christ's resurrection would not have been that cause. The mystery is fearsome: the destruction of death and the ascent of souls from Hades, which is the true hopes in God. About this hope Paul speaks, joining faith to it and bringing in love toward the one who has granted such great gifts and extends the good things forever. “These three remain,” he says: “faith, hope, love” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

In this, he says, the blessed person places hope in God and seeks eternal things, not being enticed by what appears for a short time nor turning aside from the true good to falsehood. For everything that people think they procure by themselves is falsehood; only what comes from God is true. And he demonstrated this through the whole ordering of human affairs, refuting all human things and bringing in the perfect good that comes from himself.

By speaking of himself he reveals the church, and he presents us as needing mercy so that we may remain in grace. The request for mercy is powerful, because it is said to go not to human beings but to him. For in this way we human beings obtain what comes from God: Christ, on our behalf, is the one who receives the good meant for us, as he says: “And I make a covenant with you, as my Father made with me” (Luke 22:29).

For there is no power for salvation in the church of Christ except what comes from God, since we have neither weapons nor money nor surrounding walls nor control of land nor anything of the kind that the Jews had. So it is a wonder, and no less than any of the other wonders, that people warred upon by countless nations, unarmed, unprepared, and non-resisting, remain and increase Such was the wonder of the bush that burned and was not consumed, and this was a figure of Christ conquering through suffering. For the church that suffers and is not destroyed bears in itself all the proofs of wisdom and the clear marks of help from above.

To these ends, he says, the church will advance, having first become poor and come through great poverty in the world, and having been enriched by the power that comes from you and glorified by the help that comes from you, which she asks not to delay. And because of the request it will not delay, as it is said: “The one who is coming will come and will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:3).

This psalm is also joined to the same theme. For it presents the person of the Savior, the remembrance of the passion, the prediction of the resurrection, and the return to heaven. Just now, then, he was saying: “I am poor and needy,” and it would fittingly be brought in as spoken especially by him concerning himself.

Even if understanding is good concerning all who are poor in the world for the sake of righteousness—and understanding consists in considering such poor people rich—yet the one who knows and understands the truly rich one who became poor for our sake is truly blessed. And all blessedness follows the knowledge of God.

Again the one who suffers on behalf of human beings speaks of human sins as his own, and he seeks for himself the mercy upon them that comes to us. He dissolves the contempt of those who do not know him by revealing his glory—upon himself according to his own power, and upon us according to the grace of Christ.

For this was eagerly pursued, he says, first by the invisible powers, then by the visible Jews, to cast out the true king from his natural rule, thinking to take possession of an inheritance that did not belong to them. Therefore they said: “Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12:7).
